questions.question:
**Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.**

A. It is imperative that he B. understands the severity of the situation C. and that he makes D. a clear, concise, and decisive statement to the press.

options.text: understands the severity of the situation
a clear, concise, and decisive statement to the press.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence requires the **subjunctive mood** because it begins with the phrase "**It is imperative that...**"
 
• After certain "demand" or "necessity" adjectives (such as *imperative, essential, crucial, important*) followed by "that," the verb must be in its **base form** (the infinitive without "to"), regardless of the subject.
 
• Therefore, "**understands**" should be "**understand**." (Note: Part C also contains the same error with "makes," which should be "make," but Part B is the first instance of this grammatical violation).
 
• Thus, the primary error is located in **part B** (Option 2) of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"It is imperative that he **understand** the severity of the situation and that he **make** a clear, concise, and decisive statement to the press."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **A: "It is imperative that he"** – This part correctly introduces the subjunctive clause.
 
• **C: "and that he makes"** – While this also contains a subjunctive error (it should be "make"), in multiple-choice questions, the first error or the one provided in the key option is targeted.
 
• **D: "a clear, concise, and decisive statement to the press."** – This part is grammatically correct and uses the Oxford comma and adjectives properly.
 
• **The Subjunctive Mood:** We use the base form of the verb (*be, go, work, understand*) for all persons. Example: "I suggest that he **be** on time" instead of "he is."

questions.question:
**Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.**

A. The new employee B. seems to be C. a fast learner D. and more smarter than the last one.

options.text: and more smarter than the last one

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary issue in the sentence is the use of a **double comparative** ("**more smarter**").
 
• In English, comparative adjectives are formed either by adding the suffix "**-er**" (for short words like *smart*) or by using the word "**more**" (for longer words like *intelligent*).
 
• You should never use both at the same time. Since "smarter" is already in the comparative form, "more" is redundant and grammatically incorrect.
 
• Thus, the error is located in **part D** (Option 4) of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The new employee seems to be a fast learner **and smarter than** the last one."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **A: "The new employee"** – This is the subject of the sentence and is grammatically correct.
 
• **B: "seems to be"** – This linking verb phrase correctly connects the subject to the predicate.
 
• **C: "a fast learner"** – This is a correctly structured noun phrase acting as a complement.
 
• **Comparative Rules:** Use "-er" for one-syllable adjectives (*faster, taller*). Use "more" for adjectives with three or more syllables (*more beautiful, more expensive*). For two-syllable adjectives, the rule varies, but "smarter" is the standard for "smart."

questions.question: Which of the following is the most compelling ethical argument against autonomous weapons in combat?

options.text: The potential for increased civilian casualties
The speed at which autonomous weapons operate
The transfer of life-and-death decision-making to machines
The lack of accountability in AI decisions

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 3**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Analyzing the ethical arguments in the passage:***

 
 
• The second paragraph explicitly and directly answers this question. It states: "The most compelling argument is the transfer of the life-and-death decision-making from a human to a machine."
 
• The text explains that opponents believe this is the core issue because a computer or machine lacks the "moral calculus, compassion, or comprehension of human dignity" required to make ethical judgments about taking a human life.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **The transfer of life-and-death decision-making to machines.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 (The potential for increased civilian casualties)**: Incorrect because the passage actually presents the opposite point as a *supporting* argument for the weapons: supporters contend AWS might "decrease civilian casualties" due to accuracy.
 
• **Option 2 (The speed at which autonomous weapons operate)**: Incorrect because the speed (operating with "rapidity") is listed in the first paragraph as a strategic advantage and a reason supporters favor the technology, not an argument against it.
 
• **Option 4 (The lack of accountability in AI decisions)**: Incorrect. While accountability and the "black box" of AI are major concerns discussed in the passage, the author specifically reserves the phrase "most compelling argument" for the transfer of the decision-making process itself.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the primary concern regarding the integration of AI into modern warfare?

options.text: The technology will never be able to operate in war zones
Autonomous weapons may lack the moral responsibility to make life-and-death decisions
It would be illegal under international laws of armed conflict
AI could be hacked and used against states

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Analyzing the primary concern in the passage:***

 
 
• The passage emphasizes that the core ethical dilemma is the "transfer of the life-and-death decision-making from a human to a machine."
 
• It explicitly states that opponents believe a computer "could never have the moral calculus, compassion, or comprehension of human dignity to make such judgments."
 
• Therefore, the primary concern driving the ethical debate is that autonomous weapons inherently lack the moral responsibility and human judgment required to make life-and-death decisions in combat.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Autonomous weapons may lack the moral responsibility to make life-and-death decisions.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 (The technology will never be able to operate in war zones)**: Incorrect because the passage suggests the opposite. Supporters argue AWS might "operate with more accuracy and rapidity in an unpredictable environment."
 
• **Option 3 (It would be illegal under international laws of armed conflict)**: Incorrect because while the passage notes that AWS "tests the very foundations of the international laws of armed conflict," it frames their use as a fiercely debated issue awaiting clear norms, not as an established illegality.
 
• **Option 4 (AI could be hacked and used against states)**: Incorrect because the passage focuses entirely on the ethical dilemmas of the AI's autonomous decision-making (the "black box") and accountability, rather than the threat of hacking or cyber hijacking.

questions.question: In the passage, the term "moral calculus" refers to:

options.text: The ability to make ethical decisions
The efficiency of AI systems in combat

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Analyzing the term "moral calculus":***

 
 
• In the passage, the term "moral calculus" is grouped together with "compassion" and "comprehension of human dignity."
 
• It is used to describe the uniquely human capacity that opponents argue computers lack when tasked with making life-and-death judgments.
 
• While "calculus" usually implies math, in philosophical and ethical contexts, a "moral calculus" refers to the process of weighing right and wrong, evaluating ethical variables, and arriving at a humane, ethical decision.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **The ability to make ethical decisions.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 (A complex mathematical process)**: Incorrect because the word "calculus" is being used metaphorically in an ethical sense, not literally to describe mathematics.
 
• **Option 3 (The calculation of military strategies)**: Incorrect because the passage separates strategic advantage (which AI might have) from the ethical, human judgment required to take a life (which AI lacks).
 
• **Option 4 (The efficiency of AI systems in combat)**: Incorrect because efficiency is precisely what supporters claim AI possesses, whereas "moral calculus" is specifically identified as something AI is missing.

questions.question: What is the primary ethical concern raised by the "black box" nature of AI decision-making in AWS?

options.text: It increases the speed of decision-making
It makes it difficult to assign moral and legal culpability
It reduces the potential for civilian casualties

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 3**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Analyzing the "black box" concern:***

 
 
• The passage states that the secrecy of AI's decision-making process is commonly known as a "black box."
 
• It explicitly links this "black box" nature to the "difficulty in assigning blame." Because we cannot transparently see how the machine arrived at its decision to kill, it becomes almost impossible to determine who is responsible (the programmer, the commander, or the state) if the weapon kills without authorization.
 
• Therefore, the primary ethical concern is that this opacity makes it profoundly difficult to establish moral and legal culpability.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **It makes it difficult to assign moral and legal culpability.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 (It increases the speed of decision-making)**: Incorrect because increased speed is cited as a potential strategic advantage by supporters, not an ethical concern caused by the opacity of the "black box."
 
• **Option 2 (It hinders military efficiency)**: Incorrect because the text suggests autonomous weapons might actually operate with more rapidity and accuracy, thereby potentially increasing efficiency, not hindering it.
 
• **Option 4 (It reduces the potential for civilian casualties)**: Incorrect because this is an argument used by supporters of the technology, whereas the "black box" is presented as a major ethical dilemma regarding accountability.

questions.question: Which argument in favor of autonomous weapons is most strongly supported by proponents?

options.text: They can create more humane warfare
They ensure that no human is ever at risk in combat
They act with more accuracy and rapidity

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 4**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Analyzing the proponents' arguments:***

 
 
• The passage explicitly outlines the arguments made by supporters of autonomous weapons in the first paragraph.
 
• It states: "They also might be able to operate with more **accuracy and rapidity** in an unpredictable environment, which could decrease civilian casualties."
 
• While reducing casualties is the ultimate goal, the foundational argument proponents use to support the deployment of these weapons is their inherent technical ability to act faster (rapidity) and with greater precision (accuracy) than human soldiers who suffer from fatigue, fear, and emotional stress.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **They act with more accuracy and rapidity.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 (They help reduce civilian casualties)**: Incorrect because while it is a stated benefit, the passage frames it as a secondary outcome ("which could decrease...") resulting directly from the weapons' primary attribute of operating with accuracy and rapidity.
 
• **Option 2 (They can create more humane warfare)**: Incorrect because the passage does not use this terminology. Opponents actually argue that machines lack the compassion or moral calculus to be humane.
 
• **Option 3 (They ensure that no human is ever at risk in combat)**: Incorrect because this is an absolute statement ("no human is ever at risk") that is far too extreme and is not supported by the text.

questions.question: A mixture contains milk and water in the ratio of 7:2. If the quantity of water in the mixture is 10 liters, what is the total quantity of the mixture?
questions.solution:

Logic: In a mixture, if the ratio of milk to water is given, total parts = sum of ratio parts. Quantity of water = (water’s ratio part ÷ total parts) × total quantity. Use this to find the total quantity.

Calculation:

Ratio of milk : water = 7 : 2

Total parts = 7 + 2 = 9

Let total quantity of mixture = x liters

Water’s part = (2 ÷ 9) × x = 10

x = 10 × (9 ÷ 2) = 45 liters

Hence, the correct answer is **Option 3.**

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Abdul Ghaffar Khan**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Abdul Ghaffar Khan**, also known as **Badshah Khan** or the **Frontier Gandhi**, was a prominent freedom fighter and a close associate of **Mahatma Gandhi**. 
 
• He was born on **6 February 1890**, in the **North-West Frontier Province (NWFP)**, now in **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan**. 
 
• Abdul Ghaffar Khan founded the **Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God)** movement, also known as the **Red Shirt Movement**, to promote nonviolent resistance against British rule. 
 
• He was a staunch advocate of **Hindu-Muslim unity** and followed the principles of **nonviolence (Ahimsa)** inspired by Mahatma Gandhi. 
 
• For his efforts in the Indian independence movement, he earned the title of the **Frontier Gandhi** due to his leadership in the frontier regions and his adoption of Gandhian principles. 
 
• He was the first non-Indian to receive the **Bharat Ratna**, India’s highest civilian award, in **1987**. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Khudai Khidmatgar Movement:**

• Special dishes like **Poda Pitha** (a type of baked cake) are prepared, and people engage in festivities, including playing games, singing folk songs, and enjoying traditional rituals. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Significance of Raja Festival:** 
 

• The festival is deeply connected with the agricultural and rural traditions of Odisha. It symbolizes the transition of Mother Earth to her menstruation period, a time when she rejuvenates herself. 

• It is believed that during Raja, the land should not be tilled to give Mother Earth rest, emphasizing the importance of respecting nature and its cycles. 

• The celebration of Raja also highlights the role of women in society, focusing on their health and well-being. 
 
 

• **Regional Practices:** 
 

• People in Odisha decorate swings (locally called **Ram Doli** or **Jhula**) with flowers and enjoy swinging as a form of recreation during the festival. 

• Villages organize community games and cultural programs, including traditional folk songs dedicated to Raja. 

• Markets are flooded with seasonal fruits, sweets, and items like new clothes and ornaments, making it a joyous occasion for shopping and socializing. 
 
 

• **Cultural Importance:** 
 

• Raja Festival is one of the most prominent festivals in Odisha, celebrated with enthusiasm by all communities. 

• It showcases Odisha's rich cultural heritage, including its unique cuisine, attire, and rituals. 

• The festival fosters community bonding and serves as a platform for preserving traditional practices. 
 
 

• **Comparison with Other Festivals:** 
 

• Unlike harvest festivals like **Pongal** in Tamil Nadu or **Baisakhi** in Punjab, Raja focuses on the preparation for the agricultural season rather than the culmination of harvest. 

• The emphasis on swings and women's celebration is unique to Raja and sets it apart from similar festivals in other parts of India. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Historical Background:** The term **Raja** is derived from the Sanskrit word **Rajas**, which means menstruation. This reflects the festival's connection with the fertility of Mother Earth. 

• **Geographical Spread:** While primarily celebrated in Odisha, Raja festivities have gained popularity in adjoining regions like **West Bengal** and **Jharkhand**, though on a smaller scale.

• **Modern Adaptations:** In urban areas, Raja celebrations have evolved to include contemporary entertainment like music concerts and fairs, blending tradition with modernity.

questions.question: What was the primary cause of India's 1991 economic crisis?

options.text: The government inability to repay foreign borrowings.
The state government inefficiency to not contribute to national economy.
High level of illegal migration from Pakistan and Bangladesh.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The government inability to repay foreign borrowings.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **1991 economic crisis in India** was primarily triggered by the government's **inability to repay foreign borrowings**. Due to excessive reliance on external debt to fund fiscal and trade deficits, the country faced a severe balance of payment (BoP) crisis.
 
• The **foreign exchange reserves** dropped to an alarming level of less than **$1 billion** by June 1991, which was insufficient to finance even two weeks of imports.
 
• India had accumulated a significant **current account deficit (CAD)**, caused by high imports and low exports, leading to an unsustainable external debt burden.
 
• The crisis was further aggravated by the **Gulf War (1990-91)**, which resulted in a sharp increase in oil prices, disrupting India's import bill and further depleting foreign reserves.
 
• In response, the Indian government took emergency measures, including **pledging gold reserves** to secure loans from the International Monetary Fund (**IMF**) and initiating comprehensive economic reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Background of the 1991 Economic Crisis:**

 
 
• During the 1980s, India followed an inward-looking economic strategy with high tariff barriers and import substitution policies, which led to inefficiencies and stagnation in economic growth.
 
• The fiscal deficit increased to **8.4% of GDP** in 1990-91, and the current account deficit widened to **3.1% of GDP**.
 
• Excessive reliance on external commercial borrowings made the economy vulnerable to global shocks.
 
 
 
• **Key Economic Reforms Introduced:**
 
 
• To resolve the crisis, the government launched the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)** reforms under the leadership of Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• Significant policy changes included **devaluation of the Indian Rupee**, reduction of import tariffs, deregulation of domestic industries, and opening up to foreign direct investment (FDI).
 
 
 
• **Role of International Organizations:**
 
 
• The **IMF** provided a bailout package of **$2.2 billion** to help India overcome the crisis, contingent on implementing structural economic reforms.
 
• India pledged around **67 tons of gold** to secure loans from the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan.
 
 
 
• **Consequences of the Crisis:**
 
 
• The crisis marked a turning point in India's economic policy, paving the way for a more open and market-oriented economy.
 
• India experienced accelerated economic growth in the subsequent decades, with GDP growth rates exceeding **6% annually** during the 1990s and 2000s.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Contributing Factors to the Crisis:**

 
 
• Political instability during the late 1980s and early 1990s, including the assassination of **Rajiv Gandhi** in 1991, weakened investor confidence.
 
• The Gulf War led to a significant increase in **remittances** from Indian workers in the Middle East being disrupted.
 
• India's rigid licensing system, known as the **License Raj**, stifled private sector growth and innovation.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of the 1991 Reforms:**
 
 
• Post-reform, sectors such as **IT, telecommunications, and manufacturing** emerged as drivers of economic growth.
 
• India's foreign exchange reserves grew significantly, standing at over **$600 billion** as of 2023, a stark contrast to 1991.
 
• The country transitioned from a low-growth, state-controlled economy to one of the fastest-growing major economies globally.

__
 
• The **Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT)** was established in **1991** under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India. It came into existence in the backdrop of the **economic liberalization** and reforms initiated in India in the early 1990s.
 
• It acts as the **nodal agency** responsible for implementing the **Foreign Trade Policy** of India, aimed at promoting and facilitating exports and imports.
 
• **Foreign Trade Policy (FTP)** is formulated by DGFT to enhance India's trade competitiveness globally. The policy includes guidelines for exporters and importers, along with incentives to boost trade.
 
• DGFT is headquartered in **New Delhi**, with regional offices across the country to cater to the needs of traders, exporters, and importers.
 
• It also manages the issuance of various licenses, such as **Import Export Code (IEC)**, which is mandatory for businesses engaged in international trade.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Economic Liberalization of 1991:**

 
 
• The year **1991** marked a turning point in India's economic history with the introduction of **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)** reforms.
 
• The reforms were initiated under the leadership of **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao** and **Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• The main goal was to open up the Indian economy to global markets by removing trade barriers and encouraging private sector participation.
 
• As part of these reforms, DGFT was established to promote exports and streamline trade policies.
 
 
 
• **Functions of DGFT:**
 
 
• Formulates and implements the **Foreign Trade Policy (FTP)** to enhance India's trade volume.
 
• Issues **Import Export Code (IEC)** numbers, which are essential for businesses involved in international trade.
 
• Provides various **export incentives** and schemes such as the **Advance Authorization Scheme**, **Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG)**, and **Service Export from India Scheme (SEIS)**.
 
• Handles disputes related to trade and ensures compliance with India's international trade obligations.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Trade Policy:**
 
 
• India’s **Foreign Trade Policy** is revised every five years and focuses on boosting exports and reducing trade deficits.
 
• The policy provides guidelines for exporters and importers and includes provisions for duty exemptions and incentives.
 
• For example, the **2023-2028 FTP** aims to increase India’s exports to **$2 trillion** by 2030.
 
 
 
• **Important Developments Related to DGFT:**
 
 
• Launch of **Trade Facilitation Portal**: DGFT provides an online portal for traders to access various services, such as license applications and trade data.
 
• Promotion of **Digital Initiatives**: DGFT has digitized many processes to enhance transparency and efficiency in trade operations.
 
• Alignment with **World Trade Organization (WTO)**: DGFT ensures that India's trade policies comply with global trade norms.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Import Export Code (IEC):**

 
 
• The IEC is a unique 10-digit code issued by DGFT, mandatory for all entities involved in international trade.
 
• It is needed for customs clearance, remittances, and availing export-import benefits.
 
• IEC registration has been simplified with online application processes.
 
 
 
• **Export Incentive Schemes:**
 
 
• DGFT offers various schemes like **Merchandise Export from India Scheme (MEIS)** and **Service Export from India Scheme (SEIS)** to promote exports.
 
• These schemes provide financial incentives to exporters, helping them compete in global markets.
 
 
 
• **Regional Offices:**
 
 
• DGFT operates through multiple regional offices across India to assist exporters and importers at the local level.
 
• These offices also handle trade-related grievances and provide guidance on export-import policies.
 
 
 
• **Digital Transformation:**
 
 
• DGFT has adopted digital platforms like the **DGFT Online** portal to streamline processes and enhance accessibility.
 
• It also provides online tools for export-import data analysis and policy updates.

questions.question: Which of the following veto powers is not available to the President of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Qualified Veto**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• The **President of India** exercises veto powers as per the provisions of the **Indian Constitution**. These veto powers include **Absolute Veto**, **Pocket Veto**, and **Suspensive Veto**. 
 
• **Absolute Veto:** The President uses this power to withhold assent to a bill, effectively rejecting it. This is typically exercised in cases where the bill is a private member's bill or when the cabinet resigns after passing the bill but before the President's assent. 
 
• **Pocket Veto:** The President neither gives assent nor rejects the bill, effectively delaying it indefinitely. India’s Constitution does not prescribe a time limit for this veto, making it unique compared to other countries. 
 
• **Suspensive Veto:** When a bill is sent back to the Parliament for reconsideration, except for money bills, the President exercises this veto. However, if the Parliament passes the bill again with or without amendments, the President must give assent. 
 
• **Qualified Veto:** This type of veto is not available to the President of India. It is a feature of presidential systems like that of the United States, where the President’s veto can be overridden by a two-thirds majority in both Houses of Congress. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

 
 
• **Veto Powers of the Indian President:** 
 
 
• **Absolute Veto:** Used in cases where the President outrightly rejects the bill. Example: In 1954, Dr. Rajendra Prasad withheld assent to the PEPSU Appropriation Bill. 
 
• **Pocket Veto:** This veto has been used notably by President Zail Singh in 1986 when he did not take action on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill. 
 
• **Suspensive Veto:** The President can return a bill (except money bills) for reconsideration. However, if the bill is passed again by Parliament, it is mandatory for the President to give assent. 
 
 

 
• **Veto Powers in Other Countries:** 
 
 
• **United States:** The US President exercises a **Qualified Veto**, which can be overridden by a two-thirds majority in Congress. 
 
• **United Kingdom:** The British monarchy has theoretical veto power, but it has not been exercised since the early 18th century. 
 
 

 
• **Important Points about the Indian President's Veto Powers:** 
 
 
• The President's veto powers are significant in maintaining checks and balances within the legislative process. 
 
• The **Pocket Veto** provides the Indian President with a unique form of discretion compared to other democratic nations.

questions.question: Who decides whether a bill is a Money Bill or not?

options.text: Speaker of the House of the People

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Speaker of the House of the People**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Article 110 of the Constitution of India** defines a Money Bill and explicitly states that the decision regarding whether a bill is a Money Bill or not rests with the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha**. 
 
• The Speaker's decision on this matter is considered final and cannot be challenged in any court of law. 
 
• A **Money Bill** deals with issues like taxation, borrowing of money by the government, expenditure from consolidated funds, or any financial matters as specified in the Constitution. 
 
• Only the **Lok Sabha** (House of the People) can introduce a Money Bill, and the Speaker plays a pivotal role in categorizing bills under this category. 
 
• The **Rajya Sabha** (Council of States) can make recommendations on a Money Bill but cannot amend or reject it. However, these recommendations are not binding on the Lok Sabha. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Role of the Speaker:** 
 
 
• The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is the highest authority in the Lok Sabha and is elected by its members. 
 
• The Speaker ensures the smooth functioning of the house and has the authority to interpret constitutional provisions related to parliamentary procedures. 
 
• When categorizing a bill as a Money Bill, the Speaker must ensure it adheres to the provisions mentioned in **Article 110** of the Constitution. 
 
 
 
• **Money Bill vs. Financial Bill:** 
 
 
• A **Money Bill** deals exclusively with financial matters as defined in Article 110, whereas a **Financial Bill** may involve financial aspects but also includes other legislative provisions. 
 
• Unlike a Money Bill, a Financial Bill can be introduced in either house of Parliament. 
 
 
 
• **Relevant Constitutional Articles:** 
 
 
• **Article 110:** Defines a Money Bill and its scope. 
 
• **Article 111:** Deals with the President's assent to Money Bills. 
 
• **Article 117:** Pertains to Financial Bills other than Money Bills. 
 
 
 
• **Examples of Money Bills:** 
 
 
• The **Finance Act**, which outlines taxation and expenditure policies of the government. 
 
• **GST Bills:** These were categorized as Money Bills during their passage in Parliament. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Role of the President:** The President of India cannot decide whether a bill is a Money Bill. However, the President can recommend the introduction of a Money Bill in the Lok Sabha. 
 
• **Prime Minister and Finance Minister:** While they play significant roles in drafting and proposing bills related to financial matters, they have no authority to decide if a bill is a Money Bill. 
 
• **Judicial Review:** The Speaker's decision on categorizing a Money Bill is final and cannot be subjected to judicial review. 
 
• **Historical Context:** The classification of GST Bills as Money Bills in 2017 sparked debates about the Speaker's discretionary powers in such matters.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide is transported to the lungs from all parts of the body through ______ in humans.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Blood**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Carbon dioxide (CO2)** is transported in the human body primarily through the **bloodstream**. It is carried from various tissues where it is produced to the lungs for exhalation.
 
• Approximately **70% of carbon dioxide** is transported as bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) in the blood after reacting with water and forming carbonic acid (H2CO3), which then dissociates.
 
• About **20-23%** of CO2 is bound to **hemoglobin** and transported as carbaminohemoglobin. Hemoglobin acts as a carrier for CO2, just as it does for oxygen.
 
• Only **7-10%** of CO2 is transported in the blood in a dissolved form within the plasma.
 
• CO2 is released into the alveoli of the lungs during gas exchange, where it is expelled during exhalation. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of Hemoglobin:**

 
 
• **Hemoglobin** is a protein in red blood cells that primarily transports oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. It also plays a vital role in the transport of carbon dioxide.
 
• When CO2 binds to hemoglobin, it forms **carbaminohemoglobin**. This is a reversible reaction, allowing hemoglobin to release CO2 in the lungs.
 
 
 
• **Bicarbonate Buffer System:**
 
 
• Carbon dioxide reacts with water in the presence of the enzyme **carbonic anhydrase** to form carbonic acid (H2CO3).
 
• Carbonic acid dissociates into bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) and hydrogen ions (H+) in the blood, maintaining the **pH balance** of the body.
 
• This buffering system is crucial for preventing drastic changes in blood pH levels.
 
 
 
• **Gas Exchange in the Lungs:**
 
 
• At the lungs, CO2 diffuses from the blood into the alveoli due to the **concentration gradient**.
 
• It is expelled from the body during exhalation, completing the cycle of gas exchange.
 
 
 
• **Other Transport Mechanisms:**
 
 
• While **blood** is the primary medium for CO2 transport, other bodily fluids such as **plasma** also carry dissolved CO2.
 
• Options like **sweat, mucus, and lymph** are not involved in CO2 transport as these do not serve as primary systems for respiratory gas exchange.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Respiratory System Functions:**

 
 
• The human respiratory system is responsible for the exchange of gases, including oxygen and carbon dioxide, between the body and the external environment.
 
• CO2 is a **waste product** of cellular respiration and must be removed efficiently to maintain homeostasis.
 
 
 
• **Enzyme Involvement:**
 
 
• **Carbonic anhydrase** is an enzyme found in red blood cells that facilitates the conversion of CO2 and water into carbonic acid.
 
• This enzyme accelerates the reaction, ensuring efficient CO2 transport and pH regulation.
 
 
 
• **Medical Relevance:**
 
 
• Disruptions in CO2 transport or elimination can lead to conditions such as **respiratory acidosis** or alkalosis.
 
• Understanding CO2 transport mechanisms is critical in managing respiratory and metabolic disorders.

questions.question: Mahavira Jain was born in a royal family near which ancient city?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vaishali**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mahavira Jain**, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism, was born in **Vaishali**, located in present-day Bihar, India, in a royal family of the **Kshatriya clan**.
 
• Vaishali was an ancient city renowned for its significance in both Jainism and Buddhism, and it was the capital of the **Lichchhavi Republic**, an important oligarchic republic during ancient India.
 
• Mahavira was born as Vardhamana in **599 BCE** to King Siddhartha and Queen Trishala, making Vaishali a notable historical site for followers of Jainism.
 
• Vaishali is also famous for its association with other spiritual leaders, including Lord Buddha, who delivered many discourses in the region. This emphasizes its role as a center of spiritual and philosophical growth during ancient India.
 
• Mahavira abandoned his royal privileges at the age of 30, renouncing worldly possessions and pursuing spiritual enlightenment, which eventually led him to establish Jainism as a prominent religious philosophy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Vaishali:**

 
 
• Vaishali is an ancient city located in modern-day Bihar. It was one of the world's first republics, governed by an elected assembly of representatives known as the **Lichchhavis**.
 
• It holds immense historical and religious importance due to its connection with Jainism and Buddhism. Lord Buddha preached his last sermon in Vaishali before attaining Mahaparinirvana.
 
• Vaishali is home to several archaeological sites, including the **Ashokan Pillar**, which marks the legacy of Emperor Ashoka's contribution to Buddhism.
 
 
 
• **Mahavira’s Teachings:**
 
 
• Mahavira emphasized the principles of **Ahimsa (non-violence)**, **Aparigraha (non-possessiveness)**, and **Anekantavada (pluralism)**, forming the core of Jain philosophy.
 
• He propagated the concept of the **Five Great Vows**: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness, which are followed by Jain monks and devotees.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Taxila:** Taxila, located in present-day Pakistan, was a famous center of learning in ancient India but has no direct connection to Mahavira Jain.
